differences.lead: Every child's brain works differently. These plain-language guides cover common learning differences and how short, accessible, game-based practice can fit alongside a child's own school support.
differences.intro: These guides are a starting point for families and educators, not a diagnosis. A qualified professional should always guide formal assessment and individual support.
differences.contextTitle: How an accessible practice tool can help
differences.approachTitle: Ideas to try with a child
differences.noteTitle: A note for families and educators

dyslexia.name: Dyslexia
dyslexia.issue: Dyslexia mainly affects reading, spelling and word decoding — it isn't related to a child's intelligence or effort.
dyslexia.context: Multisensory practice that pairs audio with text, broken into short, low-pressure rounds, is a widely used complement to a child's regular phonics instruction.
approach: Pair text-to-speech with reading practice so decoding isn't the only path to understanding
Keep sessions short, frequent and low-pressure rather than long and effortful
Celebrate progress and effort, not just accuracy or speed

adhd.name: ADHD
adhd.issue: ADHD affects attention, focus and impulse control, and often overlaps with reading, writing or maths difficulties.
adhd.context: Short, structured tasks with a clear goal and immediate feedback tend to work better than long, open-ended ones — a pattern many game-based practice tools are built around.
approach: Break practice into short rounds with a clear start and end
Use instant feedback (stars, XP) instead of delayed grading
Let a child switch subjects or take a break rather than push through fatigue

dyscalculia.name: Dyscalculia
dyscalculia.issue: Dyscalculia is a specific difficulty with number sense and arithmetic, separate from a child's general intelligence.
dyscalculia.context: Visual, repeated, bite-sized number practice — rather than long written problem sets — can help build number sense at a child's own pace.
approach: Practice numbers in small, repeatable chunks rather than long worksheets
Use visual and audio supports alongside written numbers
Revisit the same core skills often, rather than moving on before they're secure

dysgraphia.name: Dysgraphia
dysgraphia.issue: Dysgraphia makes the physical or cognitive process of writing difficult — it isn't a sign of low effort or carelessness.
dysgraphia.context: Digital practice that separates getting ideas down from handwriting itself can ease the physical strain while a child still practices spelling and composition.
approach: Let typing or guided on-screen input stand in for handwriting where possible
Keep writing tasks short, so fatigue doesn't overshadow the learning
Praise the ideas and effort in a piece of writing, not just its neatness

autism-spectrum.name: Autism Spectrum
autism-spectrum.issue: Autistic children have widely varying learning styles and strengths — there is no single "autism learning style" that fits every child.
autism-spectrum.context: Predictable routines, clear structure, and letting a child choose how they engage (audio, visual or hands-on) tend to support learning across the spectrum.
approach: Keep the same practice routine and structure from session to session
Offer a choice of audio, visual or interactive ways to engage with a question
Follow the child's own interests and pace rather than a fixed script

tools.h1: Learning tools and gift ideas for every child
tools.lead: Practical, honest ideas for parents, grandparents, teachers, tutors and therapists looking for gifts, toys and tools that help children learn, including children with dyslexia, ADHD, autism and other learning differences.
tools.intro: These guides describe types of tools, not brands, and Learnigo earns nothing from them. Start with what the child enjoys, and ask their teacher or therapist when in doubt.
tools.note: Learnigo does not sell products or earn money from these suggestions. They are types of tools, not endorsements: check age and safety labels, and ask the child’s teacher or therapist when unsure.

every-child.name: For every child
every-child.h1: Educational gifts and learning tools for every child
every-child.issue: The best learning gifts invite a child to play, build, read, count or move, and keep them coming back without pressure. Good tools fit the child’s interests first and the “educational” label second.
every-child.context: Mix hands-on toys with a little well-chosen screen time. Look for apps and games without ads or pay-to-win tricks, with audio support and short sessions, so learning stays relaxed for every kind of learner.
approach: Building sets, puzzles and construction toys for planning and problem solving
Board and card games that practise counting, turn-taking and reading
Audiobooks and read-along books, so stories never depend on reading speed
Art, craft and drawing kits for fine-motor skills and creativity
Active toys such as balls, a balance board or a skipping rope for movement breaks
A free, ad-free learning app such as Learnigo for short daily practice in reading, maths and science

dyslexia.name: Children with dyslexia
dyslexia.h1: Gifts and learning tools for children with dyslexia
dyslexia.issue: Children with dyslexia often love stories, ideas and building things, but decoding print takes extra effort. The most helpful tools take the strain off reading while keeping the joy of words and stories.
dyslexia.context: Look for tools that add sound, touch or movement to reading and spelling (multisensory learning), and anything that lets a child enjoy books by listening. Evidence for some popular products, such as coloured overlays, is mixed, so let the child try before you buy.
approach: Audiobooks and read-along books, so stories are never out of reach
Magnetic or wooden letter tiles for building words by hand
Phonics and word games that use sound and movement, not just print
A reading ruler or line guide, if it helps the child keep their place
Text-to-speech on a tablet or computer, and dyslexia-friendly fonts
Learnigo’s free read-aloud reading and spelling games in English Kingdom

adhd.name: Children with ADHD
adhd.h1: Gifts and learning tools for children with ADHD
adhd.issue: Children with ADHD often learn best when they can move, get quick feedback and work in short bursts. Tools that channel energy, rather than fight it, tend to work best.
adhd.context: Choose things with a clear goal and a fast payoff, and plan for movement. Visual timers and short, game-like tasks help with focus. Quiet fidget tools help some children listen while others find them distracting, so watch what works for your child.
approach: A visual timer that makes short work-and-break blocks concrete
Quiet fidget tools for listening time, chosen together with the child
A wobble cushion, balance board or exercise ball for active sitting
Fast-paced card and board games with short rounds
Noise-reducing headphones for homework in busy rooms
Learnigo’s short rounds and camera movement games for practice that moves

autism-spectrum.name: Autistic children
autism-spectrum.h1: Gifts and learning tools for autistic children
autism-spectrum.issue: Every autistic child is different, so the best gift starts with the child’s own interests and sensory preferences rather than a generic “autism toy” list.
autism-spectrum.context: Predictable, open-ended toys often work well, as do tools that make the day easier to understand. Check sensory preferences first: some children seek movement, pressure or texture, while others find noise or bright lights overwhelming.
approach: Toys and books built around the child’s special interests
Visual schedules or picture cards that make routines predictable
Sensory tools such as textured toys, putty or a swing, matched to the child’s preferences
Noise-reducing headphones for loud places
Construction sets, sorting and pattern games with clear rules
Learnigo’s predictable rounds and the camera games’ My Day and Talk & Together groups

dyscalculia.name: Children with dyscalculia
dyscalculia.h1: Gifts and learning tools for children with dyscalculia
dyscalculia.issue: Children with dyscalculia find number sense hard to grasp from symbols alone. Tools that make numbers visible, touchable and playful help quantities make sense.
dyscalculia.context: Choose hands-on maths materials and games that repeat the same core ideas in many forms, with no time pressure. Short, frequent play works better than long worksheets.
approach: Counting blocks, base-ten blocks or a bead frame to see quantities
A number line or hundred chart on the wall
Dice, dominoes and card games that practise counting without feeling like homework
Play money and a toy shop for real-world maths
A clock and a calendar to handle at home
Learnigo’s Maths Galaxy for short, visual, read-aloud number practice

dysgraphia.name: Children with dysgraphia
dysgraphia.h1: Gifts and learning tools for children with dysgraphia
dysgraphia.issue: Children with dysgraphia often have plenty to say, but handwriting is slow, tiring or hard to read. Good tools ease the physical work of writing so ideas can flow.
dysgraphia.context: Mix tools that make handwriting more comfortable with ones that let a child skip it when the goal is ideas, not penmanship. An occupational therapist can advise on grips and posture.

A slant board for a better writing angle
Raised-line or wide-ruled paper

Speech-to-text, so ideas can be dictated

dyspraxia.h1: Gifts and learning tools for children with dyspraxia
dyspraxia.issue: Children with dyspraxia (developmental coordination disorder) find planning and coordinating movement hard, from buttons and cutlery to ball games. Tools that make practice fun and repeatable help skills build up step by step.
dyspraxia.context: Choose activities that break movement into small steps, forgive mistakes and can be repeated often. An occupational therapist can suggest which skills to focus on.
approach: A balance board, stepping stones or a mini trampoline for coordination
Large soft balls and bean bags for throwing and catching
Lacing cards, threading beads and modelling dough for fine-motor skills

mixing-up-b-and-d.name: Mixing up b and d
mixing-up-b-and-d.h1: Why does my child mix up b and d?
mixing-up-b-and-d.issue: Mixing up b and d is very common while children learn to read and write, usually until about age 7 or 8. The two letters are mirror images, and young brains first learn that a thing is the same whichever way it faces. On its own, it is not a sign of dyslexia.
context: A cup is still a cup when its handle points left. Children apply the same rule to letters, so b, d, p and q can look like one shape turned around. Learning to read means switching that rule off for letters, and that takes time and plenty of practice.

Reversals usually fade as reading becomes automatic. They are worth a closer look when they carry on well past age 8 together with other difficulties, such as linking letters to sounds, remembering common words or spelling, despite good teaching.
approach: Teach one letter well first. Practise b until it is solid before working on d, so the two never compete.
Use the bed trick: write the word bed, and the b and d make the headboard and the footboard.
Link each letter to how it is written: for b, the bat comes before the ball; for d, the drum comes before the stick.
Trace big letters in the air, in sand or on a steamy window, saying the sound as you go.
Keep it light. Point out a mix-up once, calmly, and praise the corrected letter.
Read together every day. More reading is the most reliable way reversals fade.
mixing-up-b-and-d.practice: Learnigo's English rounds read every question aloud, so your child hears the sound while seeing the letter, and sound questions such as "which word starts with b?" take a few minutes, with no clock and no red marks. Camera games let children trace letters in the air. A dyslexia-friendly font and wider spacing can be switched on for the whole site.
mixing-up-b-and-d.note: Talk to your child's teacher if reversals continue past age 8, or come with other reading and spelling difficulties that are not improving. The school can look at the whole picture and, if needed, arrange an assessment.

child-hates-reading.name: A child who hates reading
child-hates-reading.h1: My child hates reading. What can I do?
child-hates-reading.issue: Most children who say they hate reading find it hard work, or have not yet found something they want to read. Take the pressure off: let them choose what to read, read aloud to them every day and keep practice short. If reading itself is a struggle, talk to their teacher.
context: Reading is slow and tiring while decoding still takes effort, so a child who sounds out most words gets little reward for a lot of work. Avoiding it is a natural response, not laziness.
Other children read well but have only met books they find dull, or feel reading is a test they can fail. Changing what and how they read often changes how they feel about it.
approach: Let them choose: comics, graphic novels, joke books, sports magazines and game guides all count as reading.
Read aloud to them every day, even after they can read alone. It builds vocabulary and shows why stories are worth the effort.
Use audiobooks alongside the printed book, so they can enjoy stories above their current reading level.
Share the reading: you read a page and they read a page, or they read only the speech bubbles.
Keep it short and regular. Ten relaxed minutes a day does more than an hour once a week.
Stop correcting every word. Let small slips go when the meaning is right, and praise the effort.
child-hates-reading.practice: Learnigo reads every question aloud, so a child who finds reading tiring can still take part and enjoy getting answers right. Rounds have ten questions, with no clock and no red marks. The AI teacher answers questions out loud, so curiosity never has to wait for reading.
child-hates-reading.note: Talk to your child's teacher if your child still struggles to sound out simple words, guesses words from their first letter, or is falling behind their class in reading. Early support makes the biggest difference.

phonics-at-home.name: Phonics at home
phonics-at-home.h1: How can I help my child with phonics at home?
phonics-at-home.issue: Follow the order your child's school teaches, keep sessions to about ten minutes, and focus on sounds rather than letter names. Say sounds cleanly ("mmm", not "muh"), blend them together to read words, and play listening games with rhymes and first sounds.
context: Phonics teaches children that letters stand for sounds and that sounds blend into words. Schools teach the sounds in a set order, so practising the same sounds at home, in the same way, helps rather than confuses.

Children first need to hear the sounds in spoken words: syllables, then rhymes, then single sounds. A child who finds phonics hard often needs more of this listening practice before letters make sense.
approach: Ask the teacher which sounds your child is learning this week, and practise those.
Say pure sounds: "sss", "mmm", "fff", without adding "uh" to the end.
Play I spy with sounds: "I spy something beginning with mmm".
Clap the syllables in names and words: but-ter-fly.
Blend aloud together, "c-a-t... cat!", then let your child try.
Read the decodable books from school together, and read richer stories aloud to them yourself.
phonics-at-home.practice: Learnigo's English Kingdom practises listening for syllables, rhymes and first and last sounds, in the order children learn them, with every question read aloud. Short spelling rounds then link the sounds to letters.
phonics-at-home.note: Talk to the teacher if your child still cannot hear rhymes or first sounds after plenty of practice, or finds blending very hard. These are early clues that extra support could help.

spelling-practice.name: Spelling practice
spelling-practice.h1: How can my child practise spelling without tears?
spelling-practice.issue: Practise a few words at a time, little and often, and say the sounds while writing. Group words by pattern (night, light, bright) instead of learning random lists, and test gently by dictating one short sentence. Celebrate what is right before fixing what is wrong.
context: English spelling is hard: the same sound can be written in several ways. Children spell best when they learn patterns and word families, not when they memorise lists letter by letter.
Spelling also depends on hearing the sounds in a word. A child who cannot yet split a word into its sounds will find spelling it much harder, so sound games are spelling practice too.
approach: Learn three to five words at a time, not twenty.
Look, say, cover, write, check: look at the word, say it, cover it, write it, then compare.
Group words by pattern: cake, make, take; night, light, bright.
Say each sound while writing it, and use letter tiles or magnetic letters when writing is tiring.
Dictate one short sentence that uses this week's words, instead of testing a list.
Point out the letters that are right first, then fix the one tricky part.
spelling-practice.practice: Learnigo's Write rounds cover short words, word families, word endings and dictation, with the word read aloud first. There are no red marks, and hints help a child reach the right answer.
spelling-practice.note: Mention it to the teacher if spelling stays far behind reading, or your child cannot spell words they read easily. Spelling that does not improve with good teaching is worth a closer look.

times-tables-at-home.name: Times tables at home
times-tables-at-home.h1: How can my child learn times tables at home?
times-tables-at-home.issue: Start with understanding and add speed later. Show multiplication as equal groups, learn the easy tables first (2, 5 and 10), and practise a little every day with games rather than long drills. Most children learn their tables over several school years, not weeks.
context: Times tables are easier to remember once a child understands what they mean. 3 × 4 is three groups of four, and seeing it with counters, coins or building bricks gives the fact something to hang on.
Patterns help too. Every answer in the 10 times table ends in 0, answers in the 5 times table end in 5 or 0, and 4 × 7 is the same as 7 × 4, which halves the facts to learn.
approach: Build groups with real objects: three plates with four grapes on each is 3 × 4.
Count in steps out loud while walking or climbing stairs: 2, 4, 6, 8.
Learn the 2, 5 and 10 tables first, then 3, 4 and 8, then the rest.
Use facts your child knows to find new ones: 6 × 4 is double 3 × 4.
Play quick games in the car or at dinner: one fact at a time, and swap who asks.
Practise a few minutes a day. Accuracy comes first; speed follows on its own.
times-tables-at-home.practice: Learnigo's Maths Galaxy practises counting in steps, number patterns and sharing into equal groups, the building blocks of times tables, with pictures before numbers, every question read aloud and no clock. Your child can also ask the AI teacher for its times tables and multiplication lessons, explained out loud.
times-tables-at-home.note: Ask the teacher for advice if your child still counts on their fingers for simple sums, finds numbers confusing or gets very anxious about maths. Some children need number sense built more slowly, and the school can help.

maths-worries.name: Worried about maths
maths-worries.h1: My child gets upset about maths. How can I help?
maths-worries.issue: Many children feel anxious about maths, often because of time pressure or a fear of being wrong. Remove the clock, treat mistakes as part of learning, use objects and pictures, and keep practice short and winnable. Avoid saying you were bad at maths yourself.
context: Maths anxiety is common and is not the same as being bad at maths. Worry takes up working memory, the mental space needed to hold numbers while working something out, so an anxious child can do worse than what they actually know.
Timed tests, being asked in front of others and adults' own worries about maths can all feed it. Calm, successful practice helps it fade.
approach: Take away time pressure. Understanding and accuracy come first.
Use real objects: coins, pasta, building bricks, measuring cups when baking.
Start each session with something your child can already do, so it begins with success.
Treat mistakes as clues: "Interesting, how did you get that?"
Spot maths in daily life: sharing a pizza, counting change, reading the clock.
Say "maths is something we get better at", and avoid "I was never good at maths either".
maths-worries.practice: Learnigo has no clock, no buzzer and no red marks. Early maths questions show pictures before numbers, and children try to beat their own best, never anyone else's score.
maths-worries.note: Talk to the teacher if your child's worry is strong, lasts, or shows up in other parts of life too. If numbers themselves stay confusing despite help, ask whether the school can look more closely at maths difficulties.

homework-and-focus.name: Homework and focus
homework-and-focus.h1: How can I make homework easier for a child who struggles to focus?
homework-and-focus.issue: Make homework short, predictable and broken into small steps. Use a fixed time and a quiet place, a visible timer for 10 to 15 minutes of work, then a movement break. Tell the teacher if homework regularly takes much longer than it should.
context: For many children, and especially children with ADHD, starting a task and keeping attention on it takes more effort than the task itself. Long, open-ended homework after a full school day is the hardest kind.
Structure does the heavy lifting: knowing what comes next, seeing how much time is left and getting quick feedback all make it easier to keep going.
approach: Same time, same place every day, with the table cleared and screens away.
Break the work into steps and write them on a list your child can tick off.
Work in short bursts of 10 to 15 minutes with a timer they can see, then move: jump, stretch, fetch a drink.
Start with the easiest task to build momentum.
Sit nearby rather than over their shoulder, and praise starting and effort, not only finishing.
Agree a stop time. If homework regularly runs over, tell the teacher.
homework-and-focus.practice: Learnigo rounds are ten questions long, with feedback after every answer, which suits short bursts. Camera games turn a movement break into play, and the Stop & Think games practise waiting, freezing and ignoring distractions.
homework-and-focus.note: If focus difficulties affect school, friendships and home life, not only homework, talk to the teacher and your family doctor. They can advise whether an assessment would help.

science-at-home.name: Science at home
science-at-home.h1: What easy science activities can we do at home?
science-at-home.issue: The best home science uses things you already have and starts with a question: will it float? Which melts first? Where do shadows go? Let your child guess first, test it, then talk about what happened. Five minutes in the kitchen or garden is enough.
context: Science for young children is about noticing, asking and testing, more than remembering facts. A child who predicts, tries and explains is doing what scientists do.
Everyday activities cover a lot of what primary schools teach: materials (floating, melting, dissolving), forces (ramps and magnets), light (shadows), plants (growing seeds) and the weather.
approach: Float or sink: test a coin, an apple, a leaf and a toy in a bowl of water. Guess first.
Melting race: put ice cubes on a plate, in a cup and in the sun. Which melts first, and why?
Grow a bean in a clear jar with damp kitchen paper and check the roots each day.
Shadow tracing: draw around a toy's shadow in the morning and again in the afternoon.
Dissolving: stir sugar, salt, sand and flour into warm (not hot) water. Which ones disappear?
Keep a simple notebook of guesses and results, with drawings.
science-at-home.practice: Learnigo's Science Lab has rounds on experiments, materials, living things, weather and the senses, all read aloud. Children can ask the AI teacher their own "why" questions and hear the answer explained.
science-at-home.note: Stay with your child for any activity with water, heat or small objects, keep small items away from younger brothers and sisters, and choose activities that suit your child's age.

learning-over-the-holidays.name: Learning over the holidays
learning-over-the-holidays.h1: How do we keep learning over the holidays without it feeling like school?
learning-over-the-holidays.issue: Build learning into everyday holiday life instead of setting worksheets. Read together, cook, play board games, go outdoors and talk. Ten or fifteen minutes of light practice a few days a week keeps skills fresh, and rest matters too.
context: Some children slip back a little in reading and maths over long breaks, although research disagrees about how much. A small amount of regular reading and number play goes a long way.
Holidays are also when children recharge. The aim is to keep the reading habit and curiosity alive, not to recreate the school day.
approach: Read every day: library trips, bedtime stories, audiobooks on car journeys.
Cook together: weighing, measuring and following a recipe are real maths and reading.
Play board and card games that use counting, money or words.
Write for a reason: a postcard, a shopping list, a holiday diary.
Go exploring: nature walks, museums, rock pools, looking at the stars.
Keep a short routine, such as ten minutes of practice after breakfast, then free time.
learning-over-the-holidays.practice: A Learnigo round takes a few minutes, so it fits into a holiday morning without taking over the day. It runs in any web browser and the site works in 14 languages, so it travels well.
learning-over-the-holidays.note: If your child is very anxious about going back to school, or found last term hard, talk to the teacher early in the new term.

choosing-a-learning-app.name: Choosing a learning app
choosing-a-learning-app.h1: How do I choose a good learning app for my child?
choosing-a-learning-app.issue: Look for an app with no adverts, no pressure to pay in the middle of a game, short sessions, and audio so your child does not have to read everything. Check what it collects about your child and whether you can see their progress. Then try it together before deciding.
context: Many apps labelled educational are designed to keep children playing rather than learning: endless levels, rewards for time spent and adverts. A good app has a clear learning goal and lets a child stop at a natural point.
Screen time is not all the same. A short, focused session on a well-made app, ideally with an adult nearby, is very different from hours of passive watching.
approach: No adverts, and no buying lives, coins or hints in the middle of a game.
Short sessions with a natural end, not endless play or streaks that punish a day off.
Audio support, and settings for text size, font and contrast.
A clear privacy policy: what is collected about your child, and can you delete it?
Progress you can see as a parent, in plain language.
Content that matches what your child is learning at school, at the right level.
choosing-a-learning-app.practice: We built Learnigo to meet this list. It is free for families, with no adverts, rounds of ten questions, every question read aloud, comfort settings for the whole site and a parent dashboard. Camera pictures never leave the device. Try it together with your child and judge for yourself.
choosing-a-learning-app.noteTitle: An app is only one part
choosing-a-learning-app.note: Even the best app is one part of learning. Reading together, talking, playing and moving matter more, and your child's teacher can suggest what suits their stage.

faq.lead: Everything families, teachers and clinicians usually ask before trying Learnigo.

items.a: Learnigo is a game-based learning platform for every child. It turns English, Maths and Science practice into short, encouraging rounds with audio support, playful visuals and instant positive feedback, adds an AI teacher and camera games, and was designed from the start with dyslexic, ADHD and other neurodivergent learners in mind.

items.q: Is Learnigo only for children with learning difficulties?
items.a: No. Learnigo is for every child and every learning setting: homes, classrooms, private tutoring and organizations. It was designed with dyslexia, ADHD and other learning differences in mind, and those same choices (short rounds, audio on every question, encouraging feedback) make learning easier and more fun for everyone.

Yes, Learnigo is free for families. Private teachers and tutors can start free and grow when they need more groups, and schools and institutes can talk to us about a plan for their whole organization.

items.q: Is Learnigo designed for children with dyslexia?
items.a: Yes, and for every other learner too. Every round is short, uses audio support alongside text, and gives instant, encouraging feedback instead of red marks, which helps dyslexic and neurodivergent learners most and every learner a little.

items.q: Can Learnigo help children with ADHD, dyscalculia or dyspraxia?
items.a: Learnigo is designed for many kinds of learners: short rounds with a clear goal suit children with ADHD, visual and repeated number practice suits dyscalculia, and the camera games give playful movement practice that families of children with dyspraxia often look for. It complements, and never replaces, professional support.

items.q: What age is Learnigo suitable for?
items.a: Learnigo is designed for children roughly aged 5 to 14, though families and educators are best placed to judge whether the pace and content suit an individual child.

items.q: What subjects can my child practice on Learnigo?
items.a: Three subjects, each with Listen, Read, Write and Speak practice: English ("English Kingdom"), Maths ("Maths Galaxy") and Science ("Science Lab"). There's also a story-based Learn mode, an AI teacher that answers questions out loud, and camera-powered games.
Yes. Learnigo uses browser-based text-to-speech so a child can complete reading content without needing to decode every word unaided.
Learnigo is available in 14 languages, switchable at any time: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, German, Dutch, Russian, Turkish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Indonesian and Vietnamese.

items.q: Do I need to install anything?
items.a: No. Learnigo runs in a web browser on computers, tablets and phones. The camera games only need a device with a webcam.

items.q: Is Learnigo a diagnostic tool for dyslexia?
items.a: No. Learnigo is an educational practice platform, not a diagnostic or medical service. A qualified local professional should guide any assessment, accommodation or individual support plan.

items.q: Can doctors and therapists recommend Learnigo to families?
items.a: Yes. Paediatricians, psychologists, occupational therapists and speech-language therapists can suggest Learnigo as free, low-pressure home practice alongside their own assessment and treatment. It is not a clinical tool and should never delay a referral.

items.q: Can schools and tutors use Learnigo?
items.a: Yes. Schools and coaching centres can sign up as an organization, with Admin and Teacher roles for managing batches, students and question content, and private teachers can run their own groups and tests.

items.q: How does my child's progress get tracked?
items.a: Automatically. Finishing a round updates XP, levels, streaks and unlockable achievement badges, all visible on a personal dashboard with an activity heatmap and progress history — nothing needs to be logged manually.
